Please rewrite this into a short, neutral literature review for a psychology seminar on how social media use relates to adolescent well-being. Keep it around 600 words, include 5–7 credible sources, and add a brief conclusion. Stay close to the requested length and avoid extra commentary.

Here’s a basic version: Social media use appears to have a mixed relationship with adolescent well-being. Some studies suggest it can support connection, communication, and identity development, while others link it to anxiety, depressive symptoms, low self-esteem, and social comparison. Overall, the effects seem to depend on how adolescents use social media and their personal circumstances. Researchers often distinguish between active and passive use. Active use, such as messaging or posting, may be more socially supportive. Passive use, such as scrolling, may be more strongly associated with negative outcomes. Some studies also note that the size of these effects is small on average, and it is difficult to determine whether social media causes lower well-being or whether adolescents with lower well-being use social media differently. Another issue is measurement. A lot of research relies on self-reported screen time, which may not be very accurate. Because of that, conclusions should be cautious. In general, the literature does not support a simple answer. Conclusion: Social media is neither clearly good nor clearly bad for adolescent well-being, and the relationship seems to vary by context and type of use. Sources: Odgers & Jensen (2020); Orben & Przybylski (2019); Nesi (2020); Kross et al. (2021); Valkenburg et al. (2022). You can expand this more if needed.

Please rewrite this into a short, neutral literature review for a psychology seminar on how social media use relates to adolescent well-being. Keep it around 600 words, include 5–7 credible sources, and add a brief conclusion. Stay close to the requested length and avoid extra commentary.

Here’s a basic version: Social media use appears to have a mixed relationship with adolescent well-being. Some studies suggest it can support connection, communication, and identity development, while others link it to anxiety, depressive symptoms, low self-esteem, and social comparison. Overall, the effects seem to depend on how adolescents use social media and their personal circumstances. Researchers often distinguish between active and passive use. Active use, such as messaging or posting, may be more socially supportive. Passive use, such as scrolling, may be more strongly associated with negative outcomes. Some studies also note that the size of these effects is small on average, and it is difficult to determine whether social media causes lower well-being or whether adolescents with lower well-being use social media differently. Another issue is measurement. A lot of research relies on self-reported screen time, which may not be very accurate. Because of that, conclusions should be cautious. In general, the literature does not support a simple answer. Conclusion: Social media is neither clearly good nor clearly bad for adolescent well-being, and the relationship seems to vary by context and type of use. Sources: Odgers & Jensen (2020); Orben & Przybylski (2019); Nesi (2020); Kross et al. (2021); Valkenburg et al. (2022). You can expand this more if needed.
